finding.summary: The gap's claim that 'No study has measured spindle trains in older adults' is false. Champetier et al. (SLEEP 2022/23) measured age-related changes in fast-spindle temporal clustering (0.02-Hz infraslow periodicity) in 147 older vs 32 young-to-middle-aged adults and related clustering to sleep-dependent memory consolidation in 57 older adults. A 2025 SLEEP study tested spindles clustered in trains as a modulator of overnight episodic memory consolidation in 42 healthy older adults, and a 2025 Sleep Advances paper characterised spindle clusters in younger vs older adults. Already answered: whether spindle clustering/trains decline with age, and whether they relate to (declarative/episodic) consolidation in older adults. Still open: whether loss of trains, rather than isolated-spindle density, mediates the age-related deficit in overnight motor-sequence consolidation, for example via reanalysis of the n=173 gross-motor PSG dataset.

resolution.reason: Accepted. Age-related changes in spindle clustering/trains, and their relation to declarative/episodic consolidation in older adults, are already studied. I removed the false 'no study has measured spindle trains in older adults' premise and the general 'do trains decline with age' component. The question now asks only whether loss of trains, rather than isolated-spindle density, statistically mediates the age deficit in overnight motor-sequence consolidation (e.g., by reanalysing the n=173 dataset).

finding.summary: The gap says 'no claim reports CLAS tested on a procedural/motor outcome in healthy older adults', but this has been done. Schneider et al. (SLEEP 2020) applied one night of auditory closed-loop SO-up-state stimulation to 17 healthy middle-aged/older adults (55.7 ± 1.0 y). Outcomes included overnight finger-tapping procedural consolidation: stimulation had no effect (t(16) = -1.01, p = .33), and SO/spindle responses were weaker than in young adults. Multi-night (3-night) PLAS has also been run in healthy older adults (mean age 68.9). It increased SO-coupled spindles by 24%, but only declarative/verbal outcomes were tested. CLAS effects on SO, spindles, coupling and motor procedural consolidation have been studied in young adults (Sleep 2023). Already answered: single-night CLAS → finger-tapping in ~56-year-olds (null), and multi-night CLAS boosting coupling in healthy older adults. Still open: multi-night CLAS with a motor-sequence outcome in adults aged 60+, and formal mediation by SO–spindle coupling.

resolution.reason: Accepted. Single-night CLAS with a finger-tapping outcome in ~56-year-olds (null), and multi-night PLAS that raises SO-coupled spindles in older adults (declarative outcomes only), are already done. I removed the false 'no CLAS on a motor outcome in older adults' premise and any single-night framing. The question now asks only about multi-night CLAS with a motor-sequence outcome in adults aged 60+, plus formal mediation through coupling.

finding.summary: The premise that open-loop nap TMR in older adults is uniformly null is mis-stated. Johnson et al. (Neurosci Lett 2020) found that TMR during a 1-h nap improved sensorimotor (non-dominant-arm throwing) accuracy in healthy older adults; the gap omits this positive result. Overnight TMR in older adults is also not untested: Cordi et al. (2018) applied overnight NREM TMR to adults over 60 (vocabulary; no benefit). Closed-loop SO-up-state TMR for motor sequences works in young adults (Nat Commun 2025). Multi-night sleep-cued TMR for motor (gait) rehabilitation is registered in older stroke and PD patients (StimuLOOP trials). Still open: phase-targeted (SO up-state) overnight TMR of a motor sequence in healthy older adults. The gap should cite the mixed (not null) older-adult TMR evidence.

resolution.reason: Accepted. Older-adult open-loop TMR evidence is mixed, not null (positive throwing-task nap TMR), and overnight open-loop TMR has been tried in adults over 60 for vocabulary. I removed the 'overnight vs nap' contrast and the 'no overnight TMR in older adults' premise, and rewrote 'why' to cite the mixed evidence. The question now asks only whether SO-up-state phase-targeted overnight TMR of a motor sequence helps healthy older adults, and whether it beats phase-random overnight cueing.

finding.summary: Training closely followed by sleep has already been compared with training far from sleep in older adults. In elderly participants, evening (6–9 pm) vs morning multi-session motor training gave better long-term retention (Front Aging Neurosci 2019). Evening finger-tapping practice in the elderly produced additional overnight and 1-week gains plus offline reorganisation, unlike morning practice (Learn Mem 2021). AOMI training at 8–10 pm ('early sleep') vs ≥12 h before sleep improved gait/balance in adults ~70 y (Sci Rep 2024; NCT05393700). This contradicts the gap's framing that the c0099 null is the main older-adult evidence. Still open: the specific within-evening manipulation (training ~1 h vs ~4 h before habitual bedtime, both tested at 24 h) in adults aged 60+, controlling time-of-testing.

resolution.reason: Accepted. Evening vs morning (and early-sleep vs ≥12 h) training has already been compared in older adults, with mostly positive results. I removed the implied broad 'training close to sleep vs far from sleep' question and the framing that c0099 is the main older-adult evidence. The question is now restricted to the within-evening ~1 h vs ~4 h before bedtime manipulation, with test clock-time matched across groups.

finding.summary: The claim that the evidence 'relies on reviews and a single small nap trial' is wrong. Siengsukon & Boyd ran overnight sleep-vs-wake (evening/morning) experiments in chronic stroke vs age-matched controls on a continuous tracking task and found sleep-dependent offline gains after stroke (Neurorehabil Neural Repair 2009). A PSG study in 20 chronic stroke patients and 10 controls related sleep parameters to offline motor learning (Front Neurol 2015). In rats, recovery of SO-coupled spindles (and loss of isolated delta waves) tracked motor recovery after stroke (Cell Rep 2022). A human pilot measured disturbed laterality of SO–spindle nesting after stroke (Front Neurol 2023). The SMiLES longitudinal study (BMJ Open 2024; NCT05746260) is underway on sleep-dependent motor-sequence consolidation after stroke. NCT05843656 (completed, n=62) applied spindle-/SO-like stimulation during sleep in stroke patients and healthy older adults with spindle-density outcomes. Still open: whether perilesional SO–spindle coupling predicts overnight paretic-hand sequence gains in chronic stroke vs healthy older controls in a circadian-matched sleep/wake design.

resolution.reason: Accepted. Overnight sleep-vs-wake offline gains in chronic stroke vs age-matched controls are documented (Siengsukon & Boyd 2009), and PSG-behaviour links exist. I removed the 'does sleep yield greater offline gains in stroke vs controls' component and the 'relies on reviews and a single nap trial' premise. The question now asks only whether measured perilesional (vs contralesional) SO–spindle coupling predicts paretic-hand discrete-sequence gains against healthy older controls in a circadian-matched design.

finding.summary: Encoding strength has already been crossed experimentally with sleep vs wake in older adults. A 2025 UMass dissertation ('Sleep Benefits Procedural Motor Learning in Older Adults With Additional Practice') assigned young (18–24) and older (62–75) adults to standard training vs overtraining on an explicit SRTT before a 12-h interval of sleep or wake. As its title says, it reports that sleep benefits procedural learning in older adults when they get additional practice. Earlier SLEEP abstracts from the same programme (2020, 2024) report the overtraining × sleep design. Already answered: whether more training restores sleep-dependent SRTT gains in older adults. Still open: training to a fixed performance criterion (rather than a fixed number of extra blocks), circadian-controlled (counterbalanced AM/PM) designs, and adequate power.

resolution.reason: Accepted. A fixed additional-practice (overtraining) × sleep/wake design in older adults already exists and reports a sleep benefit with extra practice. I removed 'does stronger encoding restore sleep gains' in general. The question now asks only whether individual criterion-based training restores gains under counterbalanced AM/PM (circadian-controlled) conditions with adequate power, since the 12-h AM/PM design confounds time of testing.

finding.summary: The gap says a circadian-controlled design showed sleep improved accuracy but not speed 'in early PD and healthy older adults'. That is a misreading of c0050–c0052. In that paper only Experiment 1 (young adults) used the circadian-controlled MEM/EME sleep-vs-wake design. Experiment 2 (26 PD and 24 healthy older controls) was an overnight pre/post design with no wake comparison, so it cannot show a sleep-specific accuracy benefit in older adults. The motivating premise therefore rests on young-adult data only. Older-adult sleep/wake studies have also reported accuracy measures (e.g., Spencer et al. 2007; Wilson et al. 2012), which bears on the claim that the nulls rest on speed alone. The proposed reanalysis by accuracy remains open but is less strongly motivated.

resolution.reason: Accepted. The older-adult/PD arm of c0052 had no wake control, so the claim of a sleep-specific accuracy benefit in older adults was a misreading. Some older-adult sleep/wake studies also report accuracy. I removed the misstated premise and the 'reanalysis will reverse the conclusion' framing. The question now asks whether a circadian-controlled sleep/wake design in older adults shows an accuracy-specific effect, and whether a systematic accuracy-vs-speed synthesis across older-adult studies changes the conclusion.

finding.summary: The between-study version of the question is partly answered. A Bayesian meta-analysis (eLife 2024/25; 23 studies, 297 effect sizes) tested coupling phase, strength, percentage and spindle amplitude as predictors of consolidation. It identified age and memory type as moderators, and found that precise, strong frontal SO–fast-spindle coupling predicts consolidation. Coupling precision vs spindle power has been compared in younger vs older adults (Sci Rep 2019, associative memory). Coupling predicts gross-motor (juggling) learning across age groups (eLife 2022). So 'does the coupling–consolidation link differ by age and task type' has meta-analytic and cross-study evidence. Still open: a within-sample test in adults aged 60+ that pits coupling against fast-spindle density as competing predictors across a motor-sequence task and a cognitive procedural task (Tower of Hanoi).

resolution.reason: Accepted. The between-study question of whether the coupling–consolidation link varies with age and memory type is addressed by the eLife Bayesian meta-analysis and cross-study work. I removed that between-study component. The question now asks only for a within-subject test in adults aged 60+ that pits coupling against fast-spindle density across a motor-sequence task and a cognitive procedural task.
